title: How to Identify Pure Sakhar: 7 Simple Tests You Can Do at Home
seoTitle: How to Identify Pure Sakhar (Jaggery): 7 Home Tests
description: Not sure if your sakhar is pure? Here are 7 jaggery tests you can do at home with water, iodine and your own hands, plus what real hill jaggery looks like.
content:
You bought a block of sakhar (jaggery) that looked perfect in the shop: smooth, golden, shiny. Then you put it in your tea and something was off. A salty edge, a strange smell, or a chalky bit sitting in the bottom of the cup.

If that has happened to you, you are not imagining things. Sakhar is one of the most commonly adulterated sweeteners in South Asia. Most of us buy it loose, by weight, with no label to read.

So here is how to identify pure jaggery at home. No laboratory. Just a glass of warm water, a few drops of iodine and your own hands: seven tests you can finish tonight, with the sakhar already sitting in your kitchen.

> To check if sakhar (jaggery) is pure, dissolve a piece in a glass of warm water. Pure jaggery dissolves fully and leaves no sediment, while adulterated jaggery leaves chalky residue at the bottom. Pure sakhar is also dark brown rather than bright yellow, and it tastes clean and sweet with no salty or bitter aftertaste.

1. [The water test](#test-1-the-water-test)
2. [The colour test](#test-2-the-colour-test)
3. [The taste test](#test-3-the-taste-test)
4. [The iodine test for starch](#test-4-the-iodine-test-for-starch)
5. [The hardness test](#test-5-the-hardness-test)
6. [The rub test](#test-6-the-rub-test)
7. [The smell test](#test-7-the-smell-test)

## What Gets Added to Sakhar, and Why

Before the tests, it helps to know what you are looking for. Four things are commonly added to jaggery, each for a reason.

**Chemical clarifiers.** When cane juice boils, a dark scum rises. Some producers add chemicals such as sulphur or washing soda to strip that scum away, because a paler batch sells faster.

**Artificial colour.** Buyers have been taught that golden jaggery is good jaggery. So dye is used to hit that shade. Sometimes it is metanil yellow, an industrial colour that is not food grade.

**Sugar syrup.** Refined sugar is cheaper than cane juice. Adding it bulks up the batch, adds weight, and makes the block harder and glassier so it survives transport.

**Chalk powder and washing soda.** These are pure weight. A few hundred grams of chalk in a sack of sakhar costs nothing and sells for full price.

None of it is done to help you. It is done for weight, for appearance and for shelf life.

Food safety authorities treat adulteration as an offence, and in Nepal the [Department of Food Technology and Quality Control](http://www.dftqc.gov.np/en/) regulates it. But loose, unlabelled sakhar sold by weight is very hard to police, so the checking has to happen in your kitchen.

If you want to see the other side of it, this is [how we boil our sakhar with nothing added](/our-story).

## Pure Sakhar Test at Home: What You Need First

Almost nothing. A clear glass, warm water, a spoon, a small bottle of tincture of iodine from any pharmacy, and clean hands. Do it near a window, where daylight tells you more than a yellow bulb.

Take two pieces if you can: the sakhar you are suspicious of, and any sample you trust. Testing side by side tells you far more than testing alone.

### One jaggery adulteration test is not enough

No single test is proof. Real sakhar varies: colour changes with the cane, the season and the fire. Run at least three of the seven tests before you decide, and trust the pattern rather than any one result.

## Test 1: The Water Test

Break off a piece about the size of your thumbnail. Drop it into a glass of warm water and stir gently. Wait two or three minutes and look at the bottom of the glass.

![Water test showing pure jaggery dissolving clear and adulterated jaggery leaving sediment at the bottom of the glass](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar/jaggery-water-test-pure-vs-adulterated.jpg "Left: our sakhar after three minutes. Right: a market sample bought the same week.")

:::compare
Pure sakhar | The water turns brown and cloudy, then clears as the piece dissolves. Nothing is left sitting at the bottom.
Adulterated | A white, grey or gritty layer settles at the bottom, or a film floats on top.
:::

**Why it works.** Cane sugar dissolves in water; chalk, sand and stone powder do not. They are heavier than water and simply fall. It is the same principle behind the household adulteration tests in the [FSSAI DART booklet](https://fssai.gov.in/book-details.php?bkid=201).

## Test 2: The Colour Test

This is the myth worth breaking first. Bright golden-yellow jaggery is not the good stuff. In most cases that shade has been helped along with a clarifier or a dye.

Natural sakhar runs from deep brown to almost black-brown. It also changes from batch to batch. The same field, boiled two weeks apart, gives two different browns.

:::compare
Pure sakhar | Dark brown, matte, slightly uneven in colour across the block.
Adulterated | Uniform bright yellow or orange, often with a glossy surface.
:::

![Comparison of natural dark brown jaggery and bright yellow chemically treated jaggery side by side](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar/dark-jaggery-vs-yellow-jaggery.jpg "Same weight, same price, very different processing.")

### Is dark jaggery better than yellow, and what does jaggery colour actually mean?

Yes, in general, but not because dark is magic. Colour is a record of how the juice was treated. Long, slow boiling over wood darkens the sugars naturally, so a dark block usually means nothing was added to stop that happening.

A pale block means the darkening was prevented. Sometimes that is careful skimming by hand. More often it is a clarifier.

**Why it works.** You are not judging the colour itself. You are judging what the colour tells you about the boiling.

## Test 3: The Taste Test

Break a small piece and let it melt on your tongue instead of chewing it. Pure sakhar is clean and sweet, with a mild caramel or smoky note at the end.

:::compare
Pure sakhar | Sweet, round, a faint caramel finish. Nothing lingers.
Adulterated | A salty edge, a bitter finish, or a flat chemical taste that stays in your mouth.
:::

**Why it works.** Excess salt is a sign the juice was over-treated during boiling, and bitterness usually comes from a clarifier that did not wash out. Your tongue notices both long before any instrument would.

## Test 4: The Iodine Test for Starch

This is the only test that needs something from the pharmacy. It is also the most conclusive. Dissolve a piece of sakhar in a little warm water, let it cool, then add two drops of tincture of iodine.

![Iodine test on jaggery solution to detect added starch](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar/jaggery-iodine-starch-test.jpg "Two drops of tincture of iodine is all it takes.")

:::compare
Pure sakhar | The solution stays brown. The iodine colour fades into it and nothing else happens.
Adulterated | The solution turns blue, blue-black or dark purple within seconds.
:::

**Why it works.** Iodine reacts with starch and turns dark blue. There is no starch in sugarcane juice, so any blue means something starchy was added for weight: flour, rice powder or arrowroot.

It is a standard household check, and the method is set out in the [FSSAI manual of quick adulteration tests](https://fssai.gov.in/).

## Test 5: The Hardness Test

Press a corner of the block with your thumb, then try to break a piece off with your fingers. You are testing how it gives way, not how strong you are.

![Testing jaggery hardness by crumbling a piece by hand](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar/jaggery-hardness-texture-test.jpg "Pure sakhar crumbles along a grain rather than snapping clean.")

:::compare
Pure sakhar | Firm, but it yields under your thumb and crumbles with a slightly grainy edge.
Adulterated | Glassy and crystal-hard. It shatters into sharp pieces instead of crumbling.
:::

**Why it works.** Added sugar syrup crystallises as the block cools, and crystals shatter. Natural sakhar keeps a little moisture and molasses in it, so it stays firm rather than brittle.

## Test 6: The Rub Test

Wet your fingertips, take a small piece and rub it between them until it starts to melt. Then look at your fingers.

![Rub test checking jaggery for chalk powder residue on wet fingers](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar/jaggery-rub-test-chalk-residue.jpg "Sticky is normal. Powdery white is not.")

:::compare
Pure sakhar | Clean, sticky and syrupy. Your fingers go brown and rinse clean.
Adulterated | A dry white or grey powder stays behind after the sticky part has melted away.
:::

**Why it works.** Sugar melts with warmth and moisture. Chalk and washing soda do not. They stay on your skin as a powder once everything around them has dissolved.

## Test 7: The Smell Test

Warm a piece in your hand for a few seconds, then hold it close to your nose. Do this before the taste test, while your senses are still fresh.

:::compare
Pure sakhar | Boiled sugarcane, a little woodsmoke from the fire, a hint of molasses.
Adulterated | Sharp, sour or faintly chemical. Sometimes there is no smell at all.
:::

**Why it works.** Smell is the first thing that goes when juice is over-processed. A block that smells of nothing has usually been stripped of the compounds that make sakhar smell like sakhar.

## How to Identify Pure Jaggery in Two Minutes

If someone in your house asks for the *sakhar chinne tarika*, the short way to know, it is this:

- Glass of warm water: does it leave sediment?
- Colour: bright yellow, or honest dark brown?
- Taste: clean and sweet, or salty and bitter?
- Iodine: does it go blue?
- Thumb: does it crumble, or shatter like glass?
- Wet fingers: sticky, or powdery white?
- Nose: sugarcane and smoke, or nothing?

![Checklist infographic of the 7 home tests to identify pure jaggery](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar/7-tests-pure-jaggery-checklist.jpg "Save this to your phone before your next shop.")

## Real vs Fake Jaggery: What Our Hill Sakhar Looks Like

We make [our chemical-free hill sakhar](/products/organic-jaggery-block) in Sankhuwasabha. The cane grows on hill terraces without chemical fertiliser or pesticide. What that hill method changes about the block in your hand, and how it differs from Terai gur, is set out in [what makes Himalayan jaggery different](/blog/himalayan-jaggery-sankhuwasabha). The juice is pressed in a kolhu, boiled in an iron kadhai over a wood fire, and poured into wooden moulds, with no sulphur, no clarifier, no colour and no added sugar.

![Traditional kolhu and iron kadhai making chemical-free sakhar in the Nepali hills](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar/traditional-jaggery-making-kolhu-nepal.jpg "The kadhai our sakhar is boiled in. Nothing goes into the juice but time and fire.")

Here is how it does against the same seven tests, honestly.

It dissolves clean, with no sediment. It stays brown under iodine. It tastes of caramel and a little smoke, it crumbles under a thumb, and it leaves your fingers sticky rather than chalky.

Now the parts we would rather not advertise. **The colour changes every batch.** Some blocks are the colour of dark chocolate, others closer to red-brown. That is the cane and the fire, not a mistake.

**It is not glossy.** A pure block looks rough and dull next to a polished market one. On the shelf, it honestly looks like the cheaper product.

**It softens in the monsoon.** In humid months it can go sticky at the edges or sweat slightly in the packet. That is moisture, and it is what unrefined sakhar does when nothing has been added to stop it.

The first time we ran the water test side by side with a market sample, our glass went brown and cleared, and theirs left a grey ring at the bottom that would not stir away. That is the day this article started.

We hold no organic certificate yet, and we would rather say that plainly than imply one. What we can tell you is how it is made and how it behaves in your glass. If you are looking for chemical-free jaggery in Nepal, you now have seven ways to check any of it, including ours.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How can I tell if jaggery is pure?

Dissolve a piece in warm water and look for sediment, then check the colour, the taste and the smell. Pure sakhar dissolves fully, is dark brown rather than bright yellow, tastes clean and sweet, and smells of boiled cane and woodsmoke. Run three tests, not one.

### Why is some jaggery dark brown and some light yellow?

Colour comes from how long the juice was boiled and whether anything was added to keep it pale. Slow wood-fired boiling darkens sugar naturally, giving deep brown. Bright, even yellow usually means a clarifier or a dye was used, or that the batch was blended with refined sugar.

### Does pure jaggery dissolve completely in water?

Yes. Cane sugar is fully water-soluble, so a piece of pure sakhar disappears into warm water leaving only brown colour behind. A gritty or chalky layer at the bottom of the glass means an insoluble filler such as chalk, sand or stone powder is present.

### Is hard jaggery better than soft jaggery?

No, hardness tells you about moisture and sugar, not quality. Glassy, crystal-hard jaggery that shatters often contains added sugar syrup. Pure sakhar is firm but crumbly and softens in humid weather, so soft is normal in monsoon and glass-hard rarely is.

### What chemicals are added to jaggery?

The common ones are clarifiers such as sulphur and washing soda, artificial colours such as metanil yellow, chalk powder as a bulking agent, and refined sugar syrup for weight and hardness. Not all are food grade. None of them are added for your benefit.

### Is shiny, bright jaggery bad?

It is a warning sign, not proof. A glossy, evenly bright block has usually been treated to look that way, because shoppers reward golden jaggery. Test it before you trust it: the water test and the iodine test will tell you far more than the shine will.

## Before You Buy Your Next Block

Pure sakhar is darker, plainer and less perfect-looking than the version most shops sell. It varies between batches, it does not shine, and it softens when the air is wet. Once you know that, the polished golden block stops looking like the better buy.

You do not need to take anyone's word for it, including ours. Water, colour, taste, iodine, thumb, fingers, nose: seven tests, ten minutes, one glass. That is how to identify pure jaggery, and it works on whatever brand is in front of you.

Once you trust the block, the next two questions are usually what it is worth and what to do with it. We have answered both: [how sakhar compares with white sugar](/blog/jaggery-vs-sugar) on calories, minerals and blood sugar, and [how to make jaggery tea without curdling the milk](/blog/jaggery-tea-without-curdling), which is where most people abandon the swap. If somebody in the house has diabetes, start instead with [whether jaggery is safe for diabetics](/blog/is-jaggery-safe-for-diabetics).

If you would like to run the seven tests on ours, [see the organic jaggery we make in Nepal](/shop), or [message us](/contact) and we will send a small piece to test against whatever is in your cupboard.

title: Sakhar vs Sugar: Which Is Actually Better for Daily Use?
seoTitle: Jaggery vs Sugar: Which Is Actually Better for Daily Use?
description: Jaggery vs sugar, compared honestly: calories, minerals and blood sugar side by side, from a sakhar producer who will also tell you where the difference ends.
content:
It is seven in the morning, the milk is already on the stove, and your hand is hovering between two jars. Sakhar or sugar? It is a small decision, and you make it every single day.

That is why *jaggery vs sugar* is one of the most asked food questions in South Asia, or *sakhar vs chini*, in the way most of us say it at home. Almost every answer online tells you the same thing: jaggery is the healthy one, white sugar is the villain.

We make sakhar (jaggery) for a living, on hill terraces in Sankhuwasabha. This article is going to tell you where the difference between them is real, where it has been badly oversold, and what we would actually do with the two jars on that shelf.

> Sakhar (jaggery) and white sugar contain almost the same calories, and both raise blood sugar. The real difference is that sakhar is unrefined, so it keeps small amounts of iron, potassium and magnesium that refined sugar loses completely. Sakhar is the better everyday choice for tea and traditional cooking, but it is still sugar, and belongs in the same small quantity.

:::table Jaggery vs sugar: how sakhar and white sugar compare
Compared on | Sakhar (jaggery) | White sugar
Processing | Unrefined. Cane juice boiled down and poured into moulds | Refined and crystallised, with the molasses removed
Calories per 100 g | Almost the same. Sakhar is mostly sucrose too, and the small gap is water and minerals, not lighter sugar | 387 kcal
Sugar content | Roughly 70 to 85 g sucrose, plus 7 to 10 g glucose and fructose | Almost pure sucrose
Minerals kept | About 0.5 to 1 g of minerals per 100 g, including iron, potassium, magnesium and calcium | Essentially none
Effect on blood sugar | Raises it | Raises it
Chemicals used | None, in traditional chemical-free production | Bleaching and clarifying agents commonly used
Taste | Caramel and woodsmoke, and it changes with the batch | Neutral, and identical every time
Shelf life | Shorter. Softens and sweats in humid weather | Very long
Best use | Tea, winter foods, traditional sweets | Baking, and anywhere a neutral taste is needed
:::

**Where these numbers come from.** The calorie figure for white sugar is the USDA FoodData Central entry for [granulated sugar](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/portal-data/external/169655). The composition figures for sakhar come from a 2021 review of non-centrifugal sugar in [Sugar Tech](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8314846/). Both are ranges, because sakhar is a farm product whose colour, hardness and mineral content shift from batch to batch, which is also why it is worth knowing [how to check whether your jaggery is pure](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar).

![Comparison chart of jaggery and white sugar on calories, minerals and processing](/blog/jaggery-vs-sugar/jaggery-vs-sugar-chart-nepal.jpg "Save this one, or send it to whoever started the argument at home.")

## First, the Honest Part: Sakhar Is Still Sugar

We sell sakhar, and we are going to open with the part that costs us sales.

Sakhar is sugar. It is cane juice boiled until the water leaves and the sugar stays, and what stays is mostly sucrose, the same sucrose that is in the white packet. The published range is about 70 to 85 grams of sucrose in every 100 grams of jaggery.

Your body does not grade sugar by how traditional it is. Sakhar raises blood glucose. So do white sugar, brown sugar, honey and the syrup in a cold drink.

The calorie difference between them is too small to change anything. Four spoons of sakhar instead of four spoons of sugar has not saved you anything worth measuring.

Elsewhere you will have read that jaggery cures anaemia, cleanses the blood or the liver, or helps you lose weight. Those claims are not supported by good evidence, and that is true of everyone's jaggery, including ours. It is a sweetener, not a medicine.

We have stood over the kadhai and watched forty litres of cane juice reduce down to a few blocks. Nothing goes into it on the way, and nothing magical goes into it either. It is cane juice with the water taken out, and it should be treated with the same respect you would give any other sugar.

If a seller tells you that you can eat more of their jaggery because it is healthy, they are selling. Eat less of it. That includes ours.

## What Actually Makes Sakhar Different

Now the real case, kept to the size it actually is.

Refining is a stripping process. White sugar is separated from the molasses that surrounds it, and the molasses is where nearly all the colour, flavour and minerals live. Sakhar is never separated from it, so what was in the cane juice mostly stays in the block.

That is why the mineral row in the table is the honest headline. Sakhar carries roughly 0.5 to 1 gram of minerals per 100 grams: iron, potassium, magnesium and calcium. Refined sugar carries essentially none.

Be careful with what that means. These are trace amounts in a food you should be eating by the spoon, not by the bowl. You would have to eat a genuinely harmful quantity of sakhar to get a useful amount of iron from it, so treat the minerals as a small bonus, never as a reason to eat more.

The second difference is what is *not* in it. Traditional sakhar is made without sulphur, without chemical clarifiers and without artificial colour, while refined sugar is routinely bleached and clarified on its way to being white. This is the difference we would actually defend, and it is [how we boil ours in Sankhuwasabha](/our-story), in an iron kadhai over a wood fire.

The third is taste, and it is not a nutrition point at all. Sakhar tastes of caramel and a little smoke, so one spoon often carries a cup of tea where two spoons of sugar were needed. Using less because the flavour is stronger is a real saving, but it comes from the habit, not from the sweetener.

![Cup of tea sweetened with sakhar beside tea sweetened with white sugar](/blog/jaggery-vs-sugar/jaggery-tea-vs-sugar-tea.jpg "Same cup, same milk. The one on the left is a shade darker and tastes of caramel.")

### Calories: is there really a difference?

Short answer: not one that matters.

Granulated white sugar is 387 kcal per 100 grams, according to USDA FoodData Central. Sakhar is mostly sucrose as well, with a little water and a small mineral fraction making up the rest of the weight, so per 100 grams it lands slightly lower.

That gap is water, not lightness. The sugar itself carries exactly the same energy in both jars.

We have not printed a calorie number for our own sakhar, because we have not had it tested, and the moisture in a hill block changes with the season. A figure copied from someone else's blog would be a guess dressed up as a fact.

The number that actually matters is not the one on a chart. It is how many spoons go into your day.

### Glycemic index: what the number does and does not mean

Glycemic index, or GI, is a measure of how fast a food raises blood glucose compared with pure glucose, which is set at 100. A lower number means a slower rise.

You will see confident GI figures for jaggery quoted all over the internet, and all of them deserve caution. Published values vary widely between studies and between batches, and researchers are still measuring it properly. There is [an ongoing trial comparing the glycemic index of different local jaggeries](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07015814).

There is a practical reason to hold the number loosely too. GI is measured by feeding someone 50 grams of carbohydrate from the food, and nobody eats 50 grams of sweetener at a sitting.

What you can safely say is this: sakhar contains the same sugars as white sugar, so it raises blood glucose in the same direction. Anyone who tells you a precise, settled GI number for jaggery is telling you more than the evidence does.

## Sakhar vs Brown Sugar vs Honey

Brown sugar surprises most people. It is usually refined white sugar with a measured amount of molasses stirred back in, so the colour is added at the end rather than kept from the beginning.

So the comparison is not really jaggery against a less-processed sugar. It is jaggery against white sugar wearing a brown coat, which is why brown sugar is so uniform in colour while real sakhar never is.

Honey is a different food with the same job. It is mostly fructose and glucose rather than sucrose, it brings its own trace compounds, and it is still a sugar that raises blood glucose. One firm safety rule: never give honey to a baby under one year old.

Sakhar's honest advantage over both is what it skips. It is not refined and re-coloured like brown sugar, and unlike almost anything on that shelf you can trace a good block back to one field and one fire.

![Sakhar jaggery compared with brown sugar and honey](/blog/jaggery-vs-sugar/jaggery-vs-brown-sugar-vs-honey.jpg "Three sweeteners, three stories, one thing in common: they are all sugar.")

## Can Diabetics Eat Sakhar?

This section is short on purpose, and we are not going to soften it.

Sakhar is a sugar and it raises blood glucose. It is not a free alternative, a safe swap or a diabetic-friendly sweetener, and nobody selling it should tell you otherwise.

That question comes up often enough, and matters enough, that we have answered it properly on its own page rather than in a paragraph here. If it is why you came, read [whether jaggery is safe for diabetics](/blog/is-jaggery-safe-for-diabetics), which covers the glycemic index claims, the gift-hamper problem and what the guidance actually says.

If you are managing diabetes, follow the guidance of your doctor or dietitian, not a blog, including this one. Your medication, your readings and your meals are specific to you in a way no article can be.

We would rather lose a sale than have someone treat our sakhar as permission to eat more sugar.

## How Much Sakhar Is Reasonable Per Day?

The clearest general guidance comes from the World Health Organization. Its [guideline on sugars intake](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549028) recommends keeping free sugars below 10% of your daily energy. Free sugars means the sugars added to food, which includes sakhar, honey and white sugar.

WHO adds that going [below 5%, or roughly 25 grams a day, about six teaspoons](https://www.who.int/news/item/04-03-2015-who-calls-on-countries-to-reduce-sugars-intake-among-adults-and-children), brings further benefit.

Put that in kitchen terms. Two spoons of sakhar in your morning chiya and two in the afternoon cup is already most of a 25-gram day, before any biscuit, mithai or cold drink.

A small piece of sakhar after a meal is a reasonable habit if the rest of the day is not sweet. Four cups of heavily sweetened tea is not, whichever jar you sweetened them from.

This is general guidance, not a prescription for you. Children, anyone with a medical condition and anyone on a controlled diet should take the number from their own doctor.

![Measured spoon of jaggery showing a reasonable daily amount](/blog/jaggery-vs-sugar/how-much-jaggery-per-day.jpg "This is what a reasonable daily habit looks like, not a bowlful.")

## How to Replace Sugar with Sakhar in Cooking

Start with a straight one-for-one swap by weight, then adjust to your taste. Most people find they end up using slightly less sakhar than the sugar they replaced, because the flavour is stronger.

For tea, do not drop a block into boiling milk. The safest method is to dissolve the sakhar in the hot water or tea first, then add the milk, or take the pan off the heat before stirring it in. Adding jaggery to milk that is still boiling hard is what makes it curdle, and [sakhar powder](/products/jaggery-powder) dissolves fastest of all. The full method, and the reason the milk splits at all, is in [how to make jaggery tea without curdling](/blog/jaggery-tea-without-curdling).

In baking, sakhar brings moisture and colour with it. Grate or powder it first so it creams properly, cut the other liquid slightly if the batter loosens, and expect a darker crumb.

It also browns faster than sugar. Drop your oven by about 10°C and check early, especially on anything thin.

Sakhar suits the things it grew up in: chiya, kheer, halwa, sesame and peanut chaku, laddu, winter sweets and anything with cardamom, ginger or ghee near it.

It does not suit everything. Meringue, whipped icing, pale cakes, delicate custards and light syrups all want a neutral, colourless sugar, and sakhar will take them brown and cloudy. Keep the white packet for those and use it without guilt.

![Sakhar dissolving in tea, showing how to substitute jaggery for sugar](/blog/jaggery-vs-sugar/jaggery-substitute-for-sugar-cooking.jpg "Dissolve it in the tea first. This is where most curdled milk comes from.")

## So, Is Jaggery Better Than Sugar?

For daily tea and traditional cooking, yes, choose sakhar. It is unrefined, a well-made block is free of the bleaching and clarifying chemicals used on white sugar, and it carries a small amount of minerals that refining removes.

For baking that needs a neutral taste or a pale colour, choose white sugar. Using the wrong sweetener to feel virtuous only ruins the dish.

For your health, the honest answer is neither. The change that helps is using less of both. If you are going to keep sweetening your chiya anyway, sakhar is the better jar to reach for.

Buy it on how it is made rather than how it looks. Bright, glossy, uniformly golden blocks are usually the treated ones, and a duller, darker, slightly uneven block is much more likely to be the real thing.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is jaggery healthier than white sugar?

Slightly, and only in specific ways. Sakhar is unrefined, so it keeps small amounts of minerals and avoids bleaching chemicals. But it has similar calories and raises blood sugar the same way, so it is a better sugar rather than a health food.

### Does jaggery have fewer calories than sugar?

Barely. White sugar is 387 kcal per 100 g, and sakhar sits slightly lower mainly because part of its weight is water and minerals. Spoon for spoon the difference is too small to matter for weight or for blood sugar.

### Can I use jaggery instead of sugar in tea every day?

Yes, if the amount stays small. Daily chiya sweetened with one spoon of sakhar is a reasonable habit within WHO's free-sugars guidance. Four heavily sweetened cups a day is not, whichever sweetener you use.

### Can someone with diabetes use jaggery instead of sugar?

No. Both are sugar and both raise blood glucose, so changing jars is not a diabetes strategy, and anyone managing diabetes should take their numbers from their own doctor or dietitian. The full answer, including what the glycemic index claims are worth, is in [is jaggery safe for diabetics](/blog/is-jaggery-safe-for-diabetics).

### How much jaggery is safe per day?

WHO recommends keeping all free sugars below 10% of daily energy, and ideally below 5%, or roughly 25 grams, about six teaspoons, from every source combined. Sakhar counts inside that limit, alongside sugar, honey, sweets and soft drinks.

### Is jaggery better than brown sugar?

Generally yes, because brown sugar is usually refined white sugar with molasses added back at the end. Sakhar was never refined in the first place, so its colour, minerals and flavour are what remained rather than what was returned.

### Does jaggery raise blood sugar?

Yes. Sakhar is mostly sucrose, the same sugar as in the white packet, so it raises blood glucose. Published glycemic index values for jaggery vary widely between studies and batches, so treat any single number you see with caution.

### Is jaggery good for weight loss?

No. Replacing sugar with jaggery will not cause weight loss, because the calories are nearly the same and both are calorie-dense sweeteners. What helps is using less sweetener overall, and the jar you use matters far less than the number of spoons.

## Jaggery vs Sugar: The Honest Verdict

Sakhar is the better daily sweetener, for smaller reasons than most sellers claim. It is unrefined, a good block is made without chemicals, and it keeps a trace of what the cane had in it. It is also still sugar, with almost the same calories, and it belongs in the same small quantity as anything else in that cupboard.

That is the whole comparison, without the marketing.

If you want to go further, learn [how to check whether your jaggery is pure](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar) before you buy another block, and [what makes hill sakhar different from Terai gur](/blog/himalayan-jaggery-sankhuwasabha) before you decide what to pay for it. Purity is where the real difference between one sakhar and another sits. And if you would like to taste the kind we make, this is [our chemical-free hill sakhar](/products/organic-jaggery-block), boiled over a wood fire in Sankhuwasabha with nothing added.

Use less of it than you think you need. We will still be here.

title: Sakhar Chiya: How to Make Jaggery Tea Without Curdling the Milk
seoTitle: How to Make Jaggery Tea Without Curdling the Milk
description: Jaggery tea curdles because acid meets boiling milk. The order that works, how much sakhar belongs in one cup, and how to rescue a pan of chiya that has split.
content:
You bought the sakhar. You dropped a piece into the pan of boiling milk, the way you have always dropped in sugar, and the whole thing turned to grey water with white flecks floating in it.

Almost everybody who tries jaggery tea for the first time does this, and most of them conclude that the jaggery was bad. It was not. The milk split because of the order you did things in, and the order is a five-second fix.

We make sakhar on hill terraces in [Sankhuwasabha](/our-story) and drink four cups of chiya a day made with it. Here is the method that never splits, the amount that actually belongs in one cup, and what to do with a pan that has already gone.

> Jaggery tea curdles because sakhar is mildly acidic and milk proteins clump when acid meets high heat. The fix is order, not better jaggery: brew the tea in water first, dissolve the sakhar in that hot liquid, take the pan off the heat, then stir the milk in last. Never drop sakhar into milk that is boiling hard.

![Two glasses of Nepali chiya side by side, one curdled and one smooth](/blog/jaggery-tea-without-curdling/jaggery-tea-curdled-vs-smooth.jpg "Same milk, same sakhar, ninety seconds apart. Only the order was different.")

## Why Jaggery Curdles Milk

Milk is a suspension of casein proteins, bundled into micelles that carry a negative charge and therefore push each other apart. That mutual repulsion is the only reason milk is a smooth liquid instead of lumps in water.

Add acid and you neutralise that charge. The micelles stop repelling each other, start sticking together, and trap the fat around them, which is the clumping you can see. The [Institute of Food Science and Technology's note on the coagulation of milk](https://www.ifst.org/sites/default/files/Coagulation%20of%20milk.pdf) sets out the mechanism properly, and it is the same one behind paneer, behind yoghurt, and behind the pan you just ruined.

Heat does not cause it on its own, but it accelerates it sharply, and it also destabilises the proteins by itself over time. Acid plus a rolling boil is the combination that splits milk in seconds.

### Where the acid in sakhar comes from

Cane juice carries its own organic acids, chiefly aconitic acid, and boiling the juice down concentrates them into the block along with the sugar. Measured jaggery sits at around [pH 5.8 to 6.4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8314846/), while fresh milk is about 6.5 to 6.7. Sakhar is therefore mildly acidic relative to the milk you are dropping it into.

Refined white sugar has had all of that stripped out, which is exactly why sugar never does this and sakhar sometimes does. A purer, better-made block is no protection either. If anything, unrefined sakhar keeps more of the cane's own acids than a treated one does, so the honest version of this product is slightly more prone to it. That is a trade we would make every time, and it is the same reason [pure sakhar softens in the monsoon](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar) while treated blocks stay hard.

### The three things that make it worse

- **A hard boil.** The higher and longer the heat after the sakhar goes in, the faster the proteins clump.
- **Milk that is close to turning.** Milk acidifies as it ages, so slightly old milk is already partway to the edge before any sakhar arrives. In a Kathmandu summer this is the usual hidden culprit.
- **Too much sakhar at once.** A heaped spoon dropped in as a lump acidifies one small area of the pan intensely before it has a chance to disperse.

## The Method That Works

This is the one to use if you want it right every time. Amounts are for one cup, and the whole thing takes about five minutes.

1. Put 100 ml water in the pan with your tea leaves, and any ginger, cardamom or cloves. Bring it to a boil and let it work for a minute or two, until the water is properly dark.
2. Take the pan off the heat. Add 1 to 1.5 teaspoons of grated sakhar or sakhar powder and stir until it has completely dissolved. Completely, with no grains left on the bottom.
3. Warm 100 ml of milk separately, or simply use it cold. Do not let it come to a hard boil.
4. Pour the milk into the sweetened tea, off the heat, stirring as it goes in.
5. Return the pan to a low flame only long enough to bring it back to drinking temperature. Take it off before it boils.
6. Strain into the glass and drink it.

The two rules doing all the work are in steps 2 and 5: the sakhar dissolves before the milk arrives, and the milk never boils hard once it is in.

![The steps of making sakhar chiya, from decoction to sweetening to adding milk](/blog/jaggery-tea-without-curdling/how-to-make-jaggery-tea-steps-nepal.jpg "Water, tea, sakhar, then milk. In that order it does not split.")

### If you prefer the traditional boil-together chiya

Plenty of Nepali kitchens boil milk, water and tea together from the start, and that is a better cup than the method above for many people. It still works with sakhar, with one change.

Boil the chiya exactly as you always do, with no sweetener in it at all. Take the pan off the heat completely. Then stir in the grated sakhar and let the residual heat dissolve it while you strain.

You can also add the sakhar in the glass instead of the pan, which is the safest version of all and the one we use when we are making one cup for one person.

## How Much Sakhar per Cup

One level teaspoon of grated sakhar is about 4 to 5 grams. Most people land on 1 to 1.5 teaspoons per cup and find that enough, because sakhar tastes of caramel and a little woodsmoke and carries a cup further than the same weight of white sugar does.

:::table One cup of sakhar chiya, by the numbers
Ingredient | Amount | Note
Water | 100 ml | Brew the leaves in this first
Full-fat milk | 100 ml | Fresh, not close to turning
CTC tea leaves | 1 heaped teaspoon | Or 1.5 for a strong Nepali cup
Sakhar | 1 to 1.5 teaspoons grated or powdered | Roughly 4 to 7 g of sugar
Ginger | A thumbnail, crushed | Into the water stage, not the milk
Cardamom | 1 pod, cracked | Optional, into the water stage
:::

Worth keeping in perspective: the World Health Organization suggests keeping free sugars [below about 25 grams a day, six teaspoons](https://www.who.int/news/item/04-03-2015-who-calls-on-countries-to-reduce-sugars-intake-among-adults-and-children), from every source combined. Two cups of chiya at 1.5 teaspoons each is already most of that before any biscuit. Sakhar counts inside that limit exactly as sugar does, which is the honest part of [our comparison of sakhar and white sugar](/blog/jaggery-vs-sugar), and the reason we tell people to use less rather than to switch and relax.

If somebody drinking this chiya has diabetes, the sweetener does not become safe by being brown. That is covered properly in [whether jaggery is safe for diabetics](/blog/is-jaggery-safe-for-diabetics), and the short version is that it is not.

## Which Form of Sakhar Dissolves Best in Tea

This matters more than people expect, because most curdling happens while a stubborn lump sits in hot milk refusing to dissolve. Hardness and moisture vary between one jaggery and another, which is largely a question of [where and how it was made](/blog/himalayan-jaggery-sankhuwasabha).

:::table How each form of sakhar behaves in a cup of chiya
Form | How it dissolves | Best for
[Sakhar powder](/products/jaggery-powder) | Fastest. Disperses almost on contact | Everyday chiya, and anyone who has curdled a pan before
[Block sakhar](/products/organic-jaggery-block) | Slowest. Grate it first, never drop a lump in | Cooking, and households that get through a kilo
:::

If you are using a block, grate it on the fine side of the grater before you start. A grated tablespoon disappears into hot tea in a few seconds; a broken lump takes a minute of stirring in exactly the conditions that split milk.

![Sakhar in powder, cube and grated block form, ready for tea](/blog/jaggery-tea-without-curdling/jaggery-forms-for-tea-powder-cubes-block.jpg "Powder for speed, cubes for portioning, block if you are grating anyway.")

## Five Mistakes That Split the Pan

1. **Dropping a lump into boiling milk.** The single most common one. Acid arrives concentrated, at maximum heat, and the milk goes in seconds.
2. **Sweetening before the milk goes in and then boiling anyway.** Dissolving early is right; boiling hard afterwards undoes it.
3. **Using milk that is a day past its best.** It is already acidic. Smell it first in warm weather.
4. **Adding lemon, ginger juice or amla to a milk chiya.** These are acids too, and they stack with the sakhar. Ginger belongs in the water stage, whole and crushed, not squeezed into the milk.
5. **Using far too much sakhar.** Beyond about two teaspoons a cup you are working against the milk as well as against your day's sugar.

## Can You Rescue a Pan That Has Already Split?

Mostly, no, and it is better to know that than to keep stirring hopefully.

If it has only just begun and you can see a slight graininess rather than proper clumps, take it off the heat immediately, stop stirring, and strain it into the glass through a fine sieve. It will be drinkable. It will not be smooth.

Once real curds have formed the tea is finished, because the proteins have set and nothing puts them back. Do not add more milk to cover it, which simply gives you more split tea.

Start again, and this time sweeten off the heat.

## Ginger, Cardamom, Masala and Black Tea

Ginger chiya is where most winter kitchens run into this, because ginger is acidic and people add it late. Crush it whole and boil it in the water stage, with the sakhar going in after the heat is off, and it behaves perfectly.

Masala chiya with cardamom, cinnamon, clove and black pepper is entirely safe. None of those are acidic enough to matter, and sakhar suits them better than white sugar does. Stir the spices into the pot with the tea leaves and sweeten with [sakhar powder](/products/jaggery-powder) at the end, off the heat.

Kalo chiya, black tea with no milk, cannot curdle at all, because there is no casein in it to clump. The same goes for lemon tea. If you want jaggery and lemon together, this is the cup to put them in, and it is the one to reach for when the milk in the house is doubtful.

![Nepali masala chiya sweetened with sakhar, with ginger and cardamom](/blog/jaggery-tea-without-curdling/masala-jaggery-tea-ginger-cardamom.jpg "Ginger goes in with the water. Sakhar goes in with the heat off.")

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why does my milk curdle when I add jaggery?

Because jaggery is mildly acidic, at about pH 5.8 to 6.4 against milk's 6.5 to 6.7, and acid neutralises the charge that keeps milk proteins apart. Heat speeds that up sharply, so jaggery dropped into hard-boiling milk curdles it within seconds.

### Can you put jaggery directly into milk?

Only into milk that is off the heat and not boiling, and even then it is safer to dissolve the jaggery in hot water or tea first. Adding it to a pan at a rolling boil is the most reliable way to split the milk.

### How much jaggery should I put in one cup of tea?

One to one and a half teaspoons of grated jaggery, roughly 4 to 7 grams, suits most people. Jaggery tastes stronger than white sugar, so start with one teaspoon and add more only if the cup needs it.

### Does jaggery powder curdle milk less than a block?

In practice yes, though the acidity is the same. Powder disperses almost instantly, so it never sits as a concentrated lump in hot milk, which is the situation that actually causes curdling.

### Is jaggery tea healthier than tea made with sugar?

A little, and not for the reasons usually claimed. Jaggery is unrefined and keeps a trace of minerals, and a well-made block is free of the bleaching used on white sugar. It is still sugar, still raises blood glucose, and still counts inside your daily limit.

### Can I make jaggery tea for someone with diabetes?

Not as a safe swap. Jaggery raises blood glucose the same way sugar does, so a cup sweetened with it has to be counted as carbohydrate and discussed with their doctor rather than treated as a diabetic-friendly option.

### Why does my jaggery tea taste bitter or burnt?

Usually because the sakhar was boiled after it dissolved, which scorches the molasses in it, or because the tea leaves were over-boiled before the sakhar went in. Sweeten off the heat and stop boiling once the milk is in.

### Can I use jaggery in black tea and lemon tea?

Yes, and these are the easiest cups of all, because there is no milk to curdle. Jaggery dissolves readily in hot black tea, and it takes lemon without any risk at all.

## The Whole Thing in One Line

Brew the tea in water, sweeten it off the heat, add the milk last, and do not let it boil again. Do that and sakhar chiya works every time, with any jaggery.

If your last block was hard to dissolve, gritty or oddly bright, the problem may not have been the method at all, so run [the seven home tests for pure jaggery](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar) on it before you blame the pan. And if you want to make this cup with sakhar boiled over a wood fire in Sankhuwasabha, with nothing added to it, [that is what we make](/shop).

title: Is Sakhar Safe for Diabetics? An Honest Answer
seoTitle: Is Jaggery Safe for Diabetics? An Honest Answer
description: Is jaggery safe for diabetics? An honest answer from a sakhar maker: what gur does to blood glucose, why online glycemic index numbers mislead, and what helps.
content:
"Chini rog cha, sakhar chalcha?" Sugar disease, in the words most Nepali families actually use. It is the question we are asked more than any other, at the stall, on the phone, and in messages that arrive at eleven at night. A daughter buying for her father. A son whose mother was diagnosed last week. Someone who has just been told to stop sugar, and wants to know whether the brown block on the shelf is allowed.

We make sakhar (jaggery) for a living, on hill terraces in Sankhuwasabha, and we would sell a great deal more of it if we gave the answer people are hoping for.

This is the other answer.

> Sakhar (jaggery) is not a safe substitute for sugar if you have diabetes. It is roughly 70 to 85 percent sucrose, the same sugar that is in the white packet, and it raises blood glucose in the same way. No good evidence shows that swapping sugar for jaggery improves blood glucose control. If you are managing diabetes, treat sakhar exactly as you would treat sugar: a small, counted amount inside the carbohydrate allowance your doctor or dietitian has given you, and never a free or health-giving alternative.

:::table What sakhar, white sugar and honey each mean for blood glucose
The question | Sakhar (jaggery) | White sugar | Honey
Mostly made of | 70 to 85 g sucrose per 100 g, plus 7 to 10 g glucose and fructose | 99.8 g sugar per 100 g, almost all sucrose | 82 g sugar per 100 g, mostly fructose and glucose
Raises blood glucose | Yes | Yes | Yes
Energy per 100 g | Close to white sugar | 387 kcal | 304 kcal
Counts as a free sugar under WHO guidance | Yes | Yes | Yes
Safe swap for someone with diabetes | No | No | No
Minerals kept | Trace, about 0.5 to 1 g per 100 g | Essentially none | Trace
Sold with health claims | Constantly | Rarely | Constantly
What to do with it | Count it as sugar | Count it as sugar | Count it as sugar
:::

**Where these numbers come from.** The composition figures for sakhar are from a 2021 review of non-centrifugal sugar in [Sugar Tech](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8314846/). The figures for white sugar and honey are the USDA FoodData Central entries for [granulated sugar](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/portal-data/external/169655) and [honey](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/portal-data/external/169640). The sakhar range is wide because it is a farm product whose moisture and mineral content shift from batch to batch, which is also why it is worth knowing [how to check whether your jaggery is pure](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar).

![Chart comparing jaggery, white sugar and honey on sugar content and effect on blood glucose](/blog/is-jaggery-safe-for-diabetics/jaggery-blood-sugar-chart-nepal.jpg "Send this to whoever told you jaggery is diabetic-friendly.")

## Why So Many People in Nepal Are Asking This

Nepal's first nationally representative survey of diabetes, run between 2016 and 2018 across 72 of the country's 77 districts, found that [8.5 percent of adults aged 20 and over were living with diabetes](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8867329/). Roughly one adult in twelve. In the same study, only about half of them knew they had it.

The [World Health Organization's diabetes fact sheet](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/diabetes) puts the same picture in global terms: cases have risen steeply for four decades, and the steepest rises are in low- and middle-income countries.

So there are hundreds of thousands of Nepali households where somebody has been told, in a ten-minute consultation, to stop eating sugar. And there is a whole shelf of products waiting to tell them that this sugar is different.

You will see blocks sold as "diabetic jaggery" and powders sold as "sugar-free gur". We have stood in a Kathmandu market and heard a seller tell a customer that jaggery cleans sugar out of the blood. That is not an exaggeration in an advertisement. It is a dangerous thing to say to somebody managing a chronic illness, and it is said every day.

## What Sakhar Actually Is, in Blood-Glucose Terms

Sakhar is cane juice with the water boiled out of it. What is left behind is mostly sucrose: about 70 to 85 grams in every 100 grams of jaggery, with another 7 to 10 grams of glucose and fructose alongside it.

Sucrose is a disaccharide. An enzyme in your small intestine splits it, within minutes, into one glucose molecule and one fructose molecule. The glucose goes straight into your bloodstream.

Your body has no way of knowing where that sucrose came from. It does not check whether the cane was grown without pesticide, whether the fire was wood or gas, or whether the block was poured into a wooden mould on a hillside in Sankhuwasabha. Sucrose from an organic hill block and sucrose from a factory sack are the same molecule and do the same thing.

That is the whole of it, and it is why every honest answer to this question has to start in the same place. We wrote a full [comparison of sakhar and white sugar](/blog/jaggery-vs-sugar) elsewhere, and the differences in it are real. None of them is a difference in what happens to your blood glucose.

## The Glycemic Index Numbers You See Online Are Not Reliable

This is where most articles about jaggery and diabetes go wrong, so it is worth slowing down.

### What glycemic index actually measures

Glycemic index, or GI, ranks how quickly a food raises blood glucose against pure glucose, which is fixed at 100. A lower number means a slower rise. It is measured by feeding volunteers a portion of the food containing 50 grams of available carbohydrate, then taking blood samples over two hours.

### Why the published jaggery numbers disagree with each other

Search for the glycemic index of jaggery and you will be given a confident figure. Search again and you will be given a different one. Published figures range from the mid-eighties down into the thirties, depending on the study, the variety of cane, how far the juice was boiled, and how much of the batch is reducing sugar rather than sucrose.

There is a good reason for that spread: jaggery is not one standardised food. Two blocks from two villages are not the same product in the way that two bags of refined sugar are. Researchers are still working on it, and there is currently [a registered trial comparing the glycemic index of different local jaggeries](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07015814).

Anyone quoting you a single precise GI number for jaggery is telling you more than the evidence supports. If that person is also selling the jaggery, treat the number as marketing.

### The measure that matters more in a real kitchen

Even a trustworthy GI number would not settle this, because GI describes a 50-gram carbohydrate portion and nobody eats 50 grams of sweetener at one sitting.

What matters at your table is how much carbohydrate actually arrives, which is glycemic load rather than glycemic index. One teaspoon of sakhar is about four to five grams of sugar. One teaspoon of white sugar is about four grams. Whatever the GI of each, the load in your cup is close to identical, because the amount is close to identical.

The honest conclusion is unglamorous. Swapping the jar changes the taste of your chiya. It does not change the arithmetic.

![Close-up of a broken block of sakhar jaggery showing its crystalline sugar structure](/blog/is-jaggery-safe-for-diabetics/jaggery-sucrose-content-close-up.jpg "Break a block open and you can see it: this is sugar, held together by a little molasses.")

## "But It Is Natural, and Unrefined"

Both of those things are true of our sakhar, and neither of them is a diabetes argument.

Unrefined is a real difference. White sugar is stripped of the molasses that surrounds it, and refined sugar is routinely bleached and clarified on the way to being white, while traditional sakhar is made with no sulphur, no clarifier and no added colour. That is the difference we would defend in public, and it is exactly [how we boil ours in Sankhuwasabha](/our-story), in an iron kadhai over a wood fire.

But "unrefined" describes what was never taken out. It does not describe a sugar that behaves differently once you have eaten it.

The minerals argument fails on dose, and it fails badly. Sakhar carries roughly half a gram to one gram of minerals per 100 grams: iron, potassium, magnesium, calcium. To get a nutritionally meaningful amount of iron from jaggery you would have to eat an amount of sugar that would harm anyone, and would harm someone with diabetes considerably faster.

Read that the other way round and it is a useful rule. If a benefit only appears at a quantity you should not be eating, it is not a benefit. It is a sales line.

## What About One Small Piece After Dal Bhat?

This is the question underneath the question, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a lecture.

A small piece of sakhar after a meal is a real habit in Nepali homes, and for somebody without diabetes it is a reasonable one. For somebody with diabetes it is neither automatically forbidden nor automatically fine. It is carbohydrate, and it has to be counted.

Two things make that harder than it sounds. The first is that dal bhat is already a high-carbohydrate meal, so the sweet at the end is landing on top of a rice load, not on an empty plate. The second is that "a small piece" is not a measurement. Broken off a block by hand, a small piece can be four grams or fourteen, and nobody weighs it.

If your doctor or dietitian has given you a carbohydrate allowance, a measured amount of sakhar can sit inside it in place of something else, not in addition to it. That is a conversation to have with them, with numbers, not a decision to make from an article. Every diabetes is different, medication and readings differ, and no page on the internet knows yours.

What we can offer is the practical half. Weigh it once on a kitchen scale so you know what a teaspoon of your sakhar actually is, and use a portioned form rather than a block, because a block invites you to break off "a little more". A level teaspoon of [sakhar powder](/products/jaggery-powder) is easier to hold yourself to than a chipped piece of block, and honestly, so is a cheap kitchen scale.

![A single small portion of jaggery weighed on a kitchen scale beside a cup of tea](/blog/is-jaggery-safe-for-diabetics/jaggery-portion-diabetes-nepal.jpg "If it is not weighed, it is not counted. This is five grams.")

## If You Are Buying Sakhar as a Gift for Someone with Diabetes

Every Dashain and Tihar we take orders from people who want to send a hamper to a parent or an in-law who has diabetes, on the understanding that jaggery is the thoughtful, healthy choice.

We would rather say this plainly than take the order quietly. Sending sakhar to somebody with diabetes as a health gift puts them in an awkward position: they either eat something they should be counting carefully, or they refuse a gift. Neither is what you intended.

If you want to send something anyway, send it as what it is, a sweet, in a small quantity, and say so on the card. Do not send it as medicine. And if the person is newly diagnosed and still working out what they can eat, send something else entirely and keep the sakhar for the rest of the family.

## What We Say to Customers Who Ask Us

We get this message often enough that we have a standard reply, and it is short.

Sakhar is sugar. It will raise your blood glucose. We do not sell a diabetic-safe jaggery, because no such thing exists, and anybody who tells you they do is either mistaken or lying. That holds for every kind of jaggery, including the [wood-fired hill sakhar we make ourselves](/blog/himalayan-jaggery-sankhuwasabha). Ask your doctor how much sugar of any kind fits into your day, then decide whether you want that amount to be ours.

We have turned down orders on the back of that message, and we would rather keep turning them down than build a business on a claim we cannot support. If you have read anywhere on our site that sakhar cures, cleanses or reverses anything, tell us and we will take it down.

## What Actually Helps

None of the following is a treatment plan, and none of it replaces the guidance you have been given by a clinician who has seen your readings.

- The clearest general target comes from the World Health Organization, whose [guideline on sugars intake](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549028) recommends keeping free sugars below 10 percent of daily energy, with [a further benefit below 5 percent, roughly 25 grams or six teaspoons a day](https://www.who.int/news/item/04-03-2015-who-calls-on-countries-to-reduce-sugars-intake-among-adults-and-children). Sakhar, honey, sugar and sweets all count inside that total.
- Learning to count carbohydrate is worth more than swapping one sweetener for another. The American Diabetes Association's explanation of [how carbohydrates work](https://diabetes.org/food-nutrition/understanding-carbs) is a plain-language place to start.
- The NHS guidance on [food and activity with type 2 diabetes](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/type-2-diabetes/food-and-keeping-active/) and the [NIDDK diabetes pages](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes) both cover the whole-diet picture that a single ingredient never will.
- If you use a glucose meter, the most honest test available to you is your own. With your doctor's knowledge, check what a measured portion of any sweetener does to your own readings, and believe that over any number quoted online, including ours.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is jaggery safe for diabetics?

No, not as a substitute for sugar. Jaggery is about 70 to 85 percent sucrose and raises blood glucose in the same way white sugar does. It is not a diabetic-friendly sweetener, and any amount needs to be counted as carbohydrate inside the allowance your doctor or dietitian has set.

### Is jaggery better than white sugar for diabetes?

Not in any way that affects blood glucose. Jaggery is unrefined and keeps a trace of minerals that refining removes, which is a genuine difference elsewhere, but both are sugar and both raise blood glucose. Swapping sugar for jaggery is not a diabetes strategy.

### What is the glycemic index of jaggery?

There is no single reliable figure. Published values vary widely between studies, cane varieties and batches, because jaggery is a farm product rather than a standardised one, and research is ongoing. Treat any precise GI number quoted by a seller with caution.

### Can a diabetic eat one piece of jaggery a day?

That depends on your medication, your readings and your carbohydrate allowance, so it is a question for your doctor rather than for an article. If it is allowed, it should be a weighed portion counted inside your day's carbohydrate, not an extra on top of it.

### Is there such a thing as sugar-free or diabetic jaggery?

No. Jaggery is made by boiling cane juice down to its sugar, so a jaggery without sugar is a contradiction. Products marketed as sugar-free or diabetic jaggery are using a claim that the ingredient cannot support.

### Does jaggery raise blood sugar immediately?

Yes. The sucrose in jaggery is split into glucose and fructose within minutes of eating it, and the glucose enters the bloodstream directly. Eating it at the end of a large meal changes the timing a little, not the outcome.

### Is jaggery good for type 2 diabetes or for reversing it?

No. There is no good evidence that jaggery treats, improves or reverses type 2 diabetes, and claims that it cleanses the blood or the pancreas are not supported. What has evidence behind it is overall diet, weight, activity and prescribed treatment.

### What should someone with diabetes use instead of jaggery?

That is a decision for your doctor or dietitian, who can weigh it against your medication and your readings. What is safe to say generally is that reducing sweetness overall does more than switching between sugar, jaggery and honey, since all three are free sugars under WHO guidance.

## The Honest Verdict

Sakhar is not safe for diabetics in the sense the question is usually asked. It is sugar. It raises blood glucose. It is not a loophole, a health food, or a gift to send to a newly diagnosed parent, and the fact that we make it does not change any of that.

What it is, for everybody else, is a better everyday sweetener than refined sugar: unrefined, chemical-free when it is made properly, and worth using in smaller amounts because the flavour goes further. That case we will make all day, and we make it in our [comparison of sakhar and white sugar](/blog/jaggery-vs-sugar).

If diabetes is not in the picture and you simply want to use less sugar in the cup you drink every morning, start with [how to make jaggery tea without curdling the milk](/blog/jaggery-tea-without-curdling), which is where most people give up on the swap. And when you want to know what is actually in the block you are buying, run [the seven home tests for pure jaggery](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar) on it first, ours included.

This article is general information, not medical advice. If you are managing diabetes, take your numbers from your doctor.

title: Himalayan Jaggery: What Makes Hill Sakhar Different
seoTitle: Himalayan Jaggery: Why Hill Sakhar Is Different
description: Wood-fired sakhar from the Sankhuwasabha hills, and how Himalayan jaggery differs from Terai gur in cane, method, colour, hardness, taste and price.
content:
The fire has been going since four in the morning. By the time the light comes over the ridge the kadhai is already loud, cane juice moving in a slow rolling boil, and the whole hillside smells of hot sugar and woodsmoke.

That smell is the part no label carries. It is also the honest starting point for a question we get asked often, usually by someone holding a block of our sakhar and a block of something cheaper from the Terai: what actually makes hill jaggery different?

We make sakhar (सख्खर, also spelled sakhkhar), or jaggery, on terraces in Sankhuwasabha in the Koshi hills. This article is our attempt to answer that properly, including the parts where the difference is smaller than we would like.

> Himalayan jaggery is unrefined cane sugar made on Nepal's hill terraces rather than on the plains. The juice is pressed, boiled in an iron kadhai over a wood fire and poured to set, with no sulphur, no chemical clarifier and no centrifuge. Compared with Terai gur it is usually darker, harder, more strongly flavoured and more expensive, because hill production is smaller and slower.

## Nepal Has No English Word for Its Own Sugar

Every place that makes unrefined cane sugar has a name that travels with it. India has gur, and jaggery in English. Colombia has panela. Mexico has piloncillo. Costa Rica has tapa dulce. Malaysia has gula Melaka. Okinawa has kokutō.

Nepal has plenty of words at home. Sakhar, gur, khudo, chaku. None of them travel. Ask for Nepali jaggery outside Nepal and you will be handed Indian gur, because that is the only word the shelf knows.

So we are using a term for it: Himalayan jaggery. We want to be exact about what we mean by that, because it is the kind of phrase that gets stuck on anything.

We mean cane sugar made in the hills, not on the plains. Indian gur is grown and boiled overwhelmingly on the Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra flats. Nepal's own volume producers are in the Terai, along the Indian border, where the land is level and the mills are large. We are on terraces in Sankhuwasabha in Koshi Province, near where the Arun comes down out of the Makalu foothills.

When we say Himalayan, it is a description of where the cane grew and where the fire was lit. It is not an adjective we added to the packaging.

## What Himalayan Jaggery Actually Is

Strip the romance out and sakhar belongs to a category with a technical name: non-centrifugal cane sugar, or NCS. The [Food and Agriculture Organization has recognised it as a distinct product since 1964](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-centrifugal_cane_sugar), and the World Customs Organization since 2007, which defines it simply as cane sugar obtained without centrifugation.

That definition is the whole thing in five words. White sugar is spun in a centrifuge to fling the molasses off the crystals. Sakhar never is. Everything that was in the juice when it went into the kadhai is still in the block when it comes out.

By composition, NCS is over 90% carbohydrate, of which sucrose is close to 80%, plus up to about 3% minerals. That is the honest nutritional shape of it, and we have written elsewhere about [what sakhar and white sugar do and do not have over each other](/blog/jaggery-vs-sugar).

The line that matters most for this article is a different one from the same source: the composition of any given NCS depends on the cane variety, the soil it grew in, how it was fertilised and how it was processed.

That is the technical reason place matters. Not folklore. Different hill, different block.

## Where It Comes From: Terraces, Not Fields

Cane on a hill terrace does not grow the way cane on a plain grows. The plots are small and cut into the slope, so nothing about the work is mechanised. Cutting is done by hand. Carrying is done on a back.

We are not going to print an altitude figure or a cane variety here. We have not had either measured properly, the terraces are not all at one height, and a number invented for a website is worth less than no number at all. When we have them we will put them on this page.

What we can tell you is what the constraint does. A terrace yields less cane than the same effort on flat ground. Everything moves slower. Nobody in the hills is running a mill at Terai scale, because there is no way to get the cane to one.

That constraint is most of the price difference, and we will come back to it.

## How Hill Sakhar Is Made, Step by Step

1. Cane is cut at first light and pressed the same day. Juice starts to ferment within hours of leaving the stalk, so this is not a step anyone can be relaxed about.
2. The juice goes into an iron kadhai over an open wood fire. Not gas, not coal, not a boiler.
3. As it heats, a foam rises. It is skimmed off by hand, repeatedly, for as long as it keeps coming.
4. The juice reduces. Forty litres becomes a few blocks. This takes hours and it cannot be hurried without scorching the batch.
5. When it reaches the right thickness, it is poured into moulds while still molten.
6. It sets in open air overnight, then it is wrapped.

Now the part that is defined by absence. No sulphur. No chemical clarifier to force the foam up faster. No bleaching agent. No added colour. No centrifuge. No anti-caking powder in the crushed version.

One point of honesty about step 3. Clarification is where a lot of jaggery gets its chemicals, and it is the step where we should be able to tell you exactly what goes into our pan and what does not. We skim, and we add nothing to speed it up. We are having the full method written down properly rather than describing it from memory on a website, and it will be published here when it is.

![Cane juice boiling in an iron kadhai over a wood fire, how Himalayan jaggery is made in Sankhuwasabha](/blog/himalayan-jaggery-sankhuwasabha/himalayan-jaggery-kadhai-wood-fire.jpg "The fire does more to the flavour than anything else in the process.")

## Hill Sakhar vs Terai Gur: An Honest Comparison

We should say plainly what this section is not. Terai gur is not a bad product. It is a good product made differently, at a scale that lets it be sold cheaply, and for a great many uses it is the sensible thing to buy.

:::table Hill sakhar and Terai gur compared on how each is grown and made
Compared on | Hill sakhar (Himalayan jaggery) | Terai gur
Where it grows | Terraces cut into hillsides, small plots | Flat land near the Indian border, large plots
Scale | Small batches, household and village level | Larger units, some approaching mill scale
Fuel | Open wood fire under an iron kadhai | Wood, bagasse or industrial fuel depending on the unit
Colour | Darker, uneven, cracks and pale streaks are normal | Often lighter and more uniform, sometimes deliberately so
Hardness | Harder. Chips rather than crumbles | Frequently softer
Moisture | Lower, in a well-reduced block | Often higher, which is part of why it is softer
Taste | Caramel and woodsmoke, and it moves between batches | Cleaner and sweeter, more consistent cup to cup
Consistency | Varies. This is a real disadvantage | More predictable, which some buyers need
Price | Higher | Lower
:::

**Where these comparisons come from.** The composition and processing differences follow from the [Sugar Tech review of non-centrifugal sugar](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8314846/) and from the FAO and WCO framing on the [non-centrifugal cane sugar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-centrifugal_cane_sugar) entry, both of which are clear that cane variety, soil and processing method drive the result. The colour, hardness and price observations are our own, from making one and buying the other.

Read that table honestly and hill sakhar loses two rows. It is less consistent and it costs more. If you are making something in volume where every batch has to behave identically, Terai gur is the better choice and we would tell you so.

## Where Nepal Sits on the World Map of Unrefined Sugar

Non-centrifugal sugar is not a South Asian curiosity. It is made in most cane-growing regions on earth, under a different name in each.

:::table Unrefined cane sugar around the world and what each one is called
Region | Local name | Usual form
Nepal, hills | Sakhar, khudo | Hard poured discs and blocks
Nepal, Terai and North India | Gur, gud | Blocks and softer lumps
India, English | Jaggery | Blocks, powder, cubes
Colombia | Panela | Moulded bricks
Mexico | Piloncillo | Small hard cones
Costa Rica | Tapa dulce | Round pressed cakes
Malaysia and Indonesia | Gula Melaka, gula jawa | Cylinders, often palm rather than cane
Philippines and elsewhere | Muscovado | Loose damp brown sugar
Okinawa | Kokutō | Hard dark lumps
:::

Nepali hill sakhar belongs on that list. It is not on it yet, mostly because nobody has been writing about it in English.

## The Vocabulary: Sakhar, Gur, Khudo, Chaku

These words get used interchangeably in shops and they should not be.

- **Sakhar (सख्खर)**, also written sakhkhar. The hill word for solid jaggery, and the word we use.
- **Gur or gud (गुड़)**. The same product, in the Terai and across northern India. If a Kathmandu shop says gud, it is usually telling you where the block came from.
- **Khudo (खुदो)**. The liquid or semi-liquid stage, sometimes sold as a syrup or molasses. We do not make it.
- **Chaku (चाकु)**. Not a raw material at all. It is a worked sweet, made *from* jaggery with ghee and often sesame, and eaten at Maghe Sankranti. We do not sell chaku either, though we will show you [how to make it](/blog/chaku-recipe-maghe-sankranti).

On the word itself: sakhar, the Hindi shakkar, the Arabic sukkar and the English *sugar* are all the same word, worn down differently over a long journey. The oldest form in the family is the Sanskrit *śarkarā*, which meant grit or gravel, presumably from what the first crystals looked like. Nepal did not borrow this vocabulary from anywhere. It is closer to the source than the English word is.

## Why Wood Fire Matters to the Taste

This is the part people expect us to oversell, so here is the size of it.

An open wood fire is uneven. Heat comes up in bursts, the pan runs hotter at the edges than in the middle, and the juice caramelises unevenly on the way down. That unevenness is exactly what produces the smoky, slightly bitter edge in a dark hill block, and the range of flavour between one batch and the next.

A controlled industrial boil does not do that, because it is not meant to. It is meant to produce the same result every time.

So wood fire is not a health claim, and anyone selling it to you as one is stretching. It is a flavour claim, and a fairly large one. It is also the reason our blocks are not identical, which some customers love and some find annoying.

## Does Nepali Hill Sakhar Deserve Origin Protection?

There is a precedent worth knowing about. [Kolhapur jaggery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolhapur_jaggery), from Maharashtra, holds a registered geographical indication. The name is legally tied to jaggery actually made in that region, in a defined way, made from unrefined juice without additives.

That is the model. It means a buyer anywhere can trust what the name says, and it means producers in that region cannot be undercut by someone printing the same word on a different product.

Nepali hill sakhar has no such protection. We do not hold a geographical indication, and we are not claiming one. We think the category deserves one, and we would rather that came from a producers' body than from any single business, including ours.

Until then, the only protection is a buyer who knows what to look for.

## How to Recognise Real Hill Sakhar

The short version, and the counter-intuitive part first: the good-looking block is usually the treated one.

A bright, glossy, uniformly golden block has often been clarified with something. A duller, darker block with cracked edges and pale streaks through it is far more likely to be the honest one. Hardness is a signal too, because a well-reduced hill block chips rather than squashes.

We have written the full version, with seven checks you can run at home using water, iodine and your own hands, in [how to identify pure sakhar](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar). If you only ever read one thing we publish before buying jaggery from anyone, make it that one.

![Dark uneven hill sakhar block beside a pale glossy block, showing how to recognise real Himalayan jaggery](/blog/himalayan-jaggery-sankhuwasabha/hill-sakhar-vs-terai-gur-colour.jpg "The one on the right looks better and is usually the one that has been helped.")

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is Himalayan jaggery?

Himalayan jaggery is unrefined cane sugar made on Nepal's hill terraces rather than on the plains. The juice is boiled in an iron kadhai over a wood fire and poured to set, without sulphur, chemical clarifiers or a centrifuge. It is a description of where and how it is made, not a grade.

### Is hill sakhar different from Terai gur?

Yes, though not in every way people assume. Hill sakhar is usually darker, harder, drier and more strongly flavoured, and it costs more because hill terraces yield less and the batches are small. Terai gur is cleaner tasting and far more consistent. Neither is a bad product.

### What does sakhar mean in English?

Sakhar is jaggery: unrefined cane sugar, sold as a solid block or crushed to a powder. Sakhar, the Hindi shakkar, the Arabic sukkar and the English word sugar all descend from the Sanskrit śarkarā, so they are the same word taking different routes.

### Is Himalayan jaggery organic?

Ours is grown without chemical fertiliser or pesticide and made without additives, which is what we mean when we say chemical-free. That is a description of our method, not a certification, and we do not hold an organic certificate. Anyone claiming certification should be able to show you the certificate.

### What is the difference between sakhar, gur, khudo and chaku?

Sakhar and gur are the same solid jaggery under a hill word and a Terai word. Khudo is the liquid or syrup stage. Chaku is a finished sweet made from jaggery with ghee and sesame, eaten at Maghe Sankranti. We make sakhar only.

### Why is hill jaggery darker?

Longer reduction over an uneven wood fire, and no clarifier or bleaching agent to lift the colour. Darker generally means the batch spent more time in the pan and carries a stronger molasses note. It is not a sign of age, and a very pale block is more suspicious than a very dark one.

### Where in Nepal is the best jaggery made?

There is no single answer, and anyone who gives you one is selling something. Hill districts across the country produce excellent small-batch sakhar, and the Terai produces good gur at a scale the hills cannot match. We make ours in Sankhuwasabha and we think it is worth the money, which is exactly what you would expect us to say.

## What Himalayan Jaggery Is, in One Paragraph

It is cane sugar made on a hillside instead of a plain, boiled over wood instead of industrial heat, and left alone instead of clarified, bleached and spun. That produces something darker, harder, more strongly flavoured and less consistent than the gur most people have had, and it costs more to make, so it costs more to buy.

If you want the cheapest sweetener in the shop, that is not us, and we would rather you knew that before you ordered than after.

If you want to taste what the fire does, this is [our sakhar block from Sankhuwasabha](/products/organic-jaggery-block), and the same batch [crushed to a powder](/products/jaggery-powder) if you sweeten your chiya daily. You can see [where it is made and who makes it](/our-story), and if you would like to know what it costs and why, that is [set out in full here](/blog/sakhar-price-in-nepal).

The fire gets lit again in the season. We will still be here.
